items.summary: This Zenodo record accompanies the paper “Scalable Measurement-Based Quantum Simulation Patterns for Benchmarking” arXiv.2605.12502   and provides QPatLib v1.0 measurement-pattern datasets in human-readable JSONL together with a ZIP archive of OpenQASM 3.0 circuits used for validation and reproducibility.  The patterns and circuits implement Pauli string unitaries  for benchmark cases.  Cases include all possible string combinations for less than 6 qubits and strings used in Hamiltonians for certain diatomic molecules for 6 or more qubits.     Format:  Each  pattern_*.jsonl file is containins measurement patterns for all subsets for a given model/instance and subset strategy: it begins with a preamble containing model metadata, subset definitions, provenance, and (when feasible) full-pattern test results, followed by one pattern entry per subset. Each subset entry includes a required  pattern_ascii field storing the measurement pattern in the measurement-calculus/Graphix standard with signal shifting, written left-to-right in the canonical order nodes → edges → measurements (with signal dependencies) → byproduct corrections (X/Z). The circuits are included as circuit_files.zip.   Patterns in this record were validated against the corresponding circuits and checked for causal flow.   Codes for generating these patterns can be found at QPatLib repository on Github

items.summary: Motivation: Variant calling for next-generation sequencing (NGS) data relies on a diverse ecosystem of tools and workflows. Large-scale collaborative studies increasingly adopt federated analysis, where each institution processes sensitive data locally using standardized pipelines. Deploying identical pipelines across multiple centers remains challenging because heterogeneous software environments and computing policies can cause workflow divergence and inconsistent results. Results: We developed CBIcall, a workflow backend-flexible, configuration-driven framework that runs standardized variant-calling pipelines from raw FASTQ files to analysis-ready VCFs. Users define each analysis in a single YAML parameters file, which CBIcall resolves against a controlled workflow registry and resource catalog. The execution driver validates parameters and checks compatibility among pipelines, analysis modes, workflow backends, genome builds, tool versions, and resource bundles. CBIcall supports reproducibility auditing by comparing executions using recorded provenance and output fingerprints. CBIcall dispatches validated workflows natively through Bash, Cromwell, Nextflow and Snakemake backends and provides production-ready pipelines for germline WES, WGS (single-sample or cohort joint genotyping following GATK Best Practices), and mitochondrial DNA analysis. We evaluated analytical performance using public benchmark datasets and validated reproducibility across four computing environments. We further deployed CBIcall in the EU HEREDITARY project, where it processed 1102 samples with both WES and mtDNA pipelines on an institutional HPC system, supporting its suitability for reproducible cohort-scale genomic analyses. Availability and implementation: CBIcall is open source (GPLv3) and distributed with ready-to-run pipelines; full dependency and installation documentation is available at https://github.com/CNAG-Biomedical-Informatics/cbicall.

items.summary: Supplementary methods, results, data tables and analysis code for the manuscript Inflammatory and NRF2-associated transcriptional responses in human intracerebral hemorrhage: paired myeloid evidence and gene-set sensitivity. The five resources contain supplementary methods, tables and figures, detailed data workbooks, reproducibility code and supporting audit documentation. Original code is licensed under MIT; original documentation and derived content are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their source terms; see LICENSES.md and source notices inside Online_Resource_3.zip. Manuscript abstract Public intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) datasets cover different tissue compartments and measure different subsets of genes, complicating comparisons across studies. We compared four specified gene sets (inflammation, complement, microglial activation and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-associated oxidative stress) in public paired human brain, single-cell and hematoma-effluent/blood datasets, using patients rather than cells as inferential units. In two studies of paired brain tissue, inflammation, complement and NRF2-associated scores were higher in perihematomal than contralateral samples in all four patient blocks and five matched pairs. Patient-level single-cell comparisons found higher inflammatory and complement scores in microglia/monocyte groups than in comparator lineages. In 14 patients with same-hour paired CD14+ and neutrophil data, a five-gene score named for microglial activation showed a positive CD14+–neutrophil local-response interaction in all 14 (adjusted P=0.000488), but four-program heterogeneity was not established (Friedman P=0.0796). Restricting this score to three shared genes reversed its CD14+ local response; a jointly scaled three-gene interaction was near zero. Independent acute blood data showed positive case-control differences, whereas longitudinal changes were not significant after adjustment. Inflammatory and NRF2-associated expression differences recurred across these datasets. The CD14+ local response of the microglial-related score depended on its measured genes. Version 2026-10-24 changes This revision aligns the five supplementary resources with the current manuscript and adds the exact GSE163256 primary fractional-count-to-score reconstruction and fresh-score downstream verification. Earlier domain-score displays in Online Resource 2, worksheets 05 and 06, are replaced by the fixed-program paired-brain results already used in the manuscript. Superseded, undocumented competitive-null fields are removed from the current Puy13 summary display and export; the defined manufacturer-panel-matched analysis is retained. Scoring and provenance descriptions, archive entry points, fonts, table formatting and numerical display precision have also been corrected. The primary biological scores and current inferential statistics are unchanged. Earlier inputs and execution records are retained with their historical roles identified.

items.summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. items.summary: Large organizations increasingly face what this book calls the cognitive complexity wall: at the scale of hundreds of interacting components, maintaining the dependency map and reacting at the pace of incidents exceeds what a human team can deliver. This conceptual volume proposes AAM/5C, in which five capabilities (Capture, Comprehend, Choose, Coordinate, Control) are instantiated across seven logical layers, L1 to L7. A single authorization rule, R-AUT, separates who proposes, who decides and who executes: a probabilistic planner (L4) proposes; a governance layer (L6) decides under signed policies and records its verdict in a signed evaluation proof; a security layer (L5) issues a short-lived act token bound to that proof; a policy enforcement point verifies both before the target layer materializes the act. Under an explicit guarantee contract, two analytical statements (H7a, H8a) hold by construction. The other statements of its ten hypotheses (H1 to H10), including log completeness (H7b) and non-bypass of the enforcement point (H8b), are refutable, and the protocol that could refute them is fixed before any measurement. The contribution of the book is a prescriptive reference model that articulates, under this single authorization rule, known mechanisms and adds three constructs, all to be validated: the Validation step of the Distributed Autonomy Loop, the ephemeral authority surface and the cognitive dependency plane. The book positions them against autonomic computing, multi-agent systems, enterprise architecture and agent protocols (MCP, A2A), gives an authorization policy in Rego and a partial TLA+ specification of peer consensus, and sets out a validation program with quantified milestones. It reports no empirical results. This English edition is a translation of the French original, produced with the assistance of AI tools and validated by the author.
items.title: Agentic Architecture of Information Systems. The AAM/5C Model: A Reference Model for Distributed Autonomy

items.summary: Overview This repository contains the replication data, source code, execution logs, and complete analytical outputs for the study: “Detectability of controlled leaks in an Andean water transmission main: a field evaluation of changepoint methods on flow and pressure signals.” The study evaluates the detectability of short-duration controlled leaks using five changepoint and anomaly-detection approaches applied to 30-second flow and pressure measurements collected during two field campaigns in an operational water transmission main in Loja, Ecuador. The evaluated methods are: Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Bayesian Information Criterion (PELT-BIC), Pruned Exact Linear Time using the Akaike Information Criterion (PELT-AIC), Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCD), Cumulative Sum control charts (CUSUM), Moving-average ±3σ control-chart baseline. The repository contains the complete workflow used to: verify field records and ground-truth leak timings; perform campaign-specific spectral analyses using multitaper estimation; evaluate changepoint-detection performance; quantify event-level leak detectability; compare observed performance against chance-level expectations; assess BOCD sensitivity to hazard-rate and threshold settings; generate precision-recall curves and average-precision statistics; perform cross-campaign validation analyses; estimate theoretical detection-delay bounds for flow-based detection. This version supersedes earlier releases by correcting changepoint-index alignment, revising false-alarm-rate calculations using exposure time outside detection windows, replacing pooled spectral analyses with campaign-specific multitaper analyses, and incorporating event-level detectability, chance-level benchmarking, precision-recall evaluation, cross-campaign validation, and theoretical detection-delay analyses. items.summary: This Zenodo record accompanies the paper “Scalable Measurement-Based Quantum Simulation Patterns for Benchmarking” arXiv.2605.12502   and provides QPatLib v1.0 measurement-pattern datasets in human-readable JSONL together with a ZIP archive of OpenQASM 3.0 circuits used for validation and reproducibility.  The patterns and circuits implement Pauli string unitaries  for benchmark cases.  Cases include all possible string combinations for less than 6 qubits and strings used in Hamiltonians for certain diatomic molecules for 6 or more qubits.     Format:  Each  pattern_*.jsonl file is containins measurement patterns for all subsets for a given model/instance and subset strategy: it begins with a preamble containing model metadata, subset definitions, provenance, and (when feasible) full-pattern test results, followed by one pattern entry per subset. Each subset entry includes a required  pattern_ascii field storing the measurement pattern in the measurement-calculus/Graphix standard with signal shifting, written left-to-right in the canonical order nodes → edges → measurements (with signal dependencies) → byproduct corrections (X/Z). The circuits are included as circuit_files.zip.   Patterns in this record were validated against the corresponding circuits and checked for causal flow.   Codes for generating these patterns can be found at QPatLib repository on Github
items.title: QPatLib v1.0 — Measurement-based quantum simulation Pauli string unitary pattern collections

items.summary: HBB2OBB converts horizontal (axis-aligned) bounding boxes (HBBs) into oriented (rotated) bounding boxes (OBBs) by using existing HBB annotations as prompts for segmentation models from the SAM (Segment Anything Model) family. It targets object detection tasks where objects appear at arbitrary orientations, such as aerial imagery, satellite data, and traffic monitoring, producing oriented boxes that tightly encapsulate non-upright objects without any re-annotation. Beyond conversion, it provides horizontal box detection, evaluation, hyperparameter optimization, an interactive annotation viewer, and annotation format-conversion tools, exposed through both a command-line interface and a Python API. 📖 Documentation: rfonod.github.io/hbb2obb , with a quick start on the bundled sample data, a guide per command, pages on how the conversion works, the confidence score, the metrics and provenance, and a CLI and API reference generated from the code. Why HBB2OBB 🎯 Accurate OBBs from HBBs : prompts SAM-family segmentation models with existing horizontal boxes to fit tight oriented boxes around non-upright objects, with no re-annotation required. 🚗 No HBBs? Detect them : the hbb2obb-detect command runs an Ultralytics detector over the images and writes the horizontal boxes the conversion consumes, confidence column included. 🧩 Model ensemble : combines masks from multiple SAM variants through majority voting for more robust, accurate results. 🛡️ Spatially constrained and safe : region-specific masking and contour refinement keep segmentation inside the object, a mask split by an occluder is fitted back together, and a fallback retains the original HBB when no valid mask is found, counted and reported rather than left to be discovered afterwards. 🔎 Confidence-scored output : every OBB receives a heuristic quality score in [0, 1] that flags silent fallbacks and low-confidence conversions, so you know which boxes to trust; the scores go in the label files or in a side-car directory that keeps them strictly standard, and the detector's own confidence can be carried through instead of, or on top of, that score. 📐 Flexible scaling : positive or negative scale factors, optionally different for the short and long sides, recover cropped object parts or tighten overly conservative annotations. 📊 Evaluate and optimize : evaluation against ground truth on IoU, orientation error, and the share of boxes above a high IoU bar, plus the hbb2obb-optimize command, a hyperparameter search over SAM inference resolution, scale factors, and morphological opening kernel, driven by a configuration file so that a whole benchmark of model ensembles is a single reproducible command. 🔬 Where the score comes from : the hbb2obb-analyze command breaks one evaluation down by the ground truth's orientation, size, frame edge, difficulty and class, and scores the conversion against emitting the horizontal prompt unchanged. 🔄 Five annotation formats : read and write YOLO, DOTA, Pascal VOC, COCO, and LabelMe, for horizontal and oriented boxes alike, with a check that proves every format encodes the same boxes. 🔍 Interactive viewer : the hbb2obb-view command pans and zooms over the annotations, in any format, coloring boxes by confidence and overlaying predictions against ground truth. Where a set ships the same boxes several ways, it names the format on screen and switches between them on a keypress. Features HBB to OBB conversion of YOLO-format annotations using SAM-based segmentation, written in absolute pixels or, with --normalize , relative to [0, 1], the convention Ultralytics reads. HBB detection : produce the horizontal boxes in the first place with any Ultralytics detector, a local file, a link, the Ultralytics catalogue, or Hugging Face, passing any other predictor argument straight through. Multiple model support : SAM, SAM2, SAM2.1, SAM3, Mobile SAM, and FastSAM families. Model ensemble via majority voting for enhanced accuracy. Confidence scoring : a per-OBB quali

items.summary: Every LLM request SWAN AI-SQL (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWAN-AISQL) and the baselines issue on SemBench MOVIE/ECOMM/MMQA, the 30-query hybrid bench of the PLOP paper and the SWAN 2.0 benchmark (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWANBench), with the provider's answer, its measured latency and its cost, as a DuckDB file (gzip-compressed, 0.96 GB; 4.4 GB unpacked; 2,409,502 recorded calls) for the repository's cache proxy (serve/ai_cache_server.py). It holds SWAN AI-SQL, LOTUS 1.2.4, PLOP (the public Morrila fork, DP cost-model mode), BlendSQL 0.1.27, ThalamusDB 0.1.15 (exact mode) and Palimpzest 1.5.3 (Abacus optimizer) on every benchmark each of them runs. SWAN AI-SQL's recordings are its current ones (2026-10-23, DuckDB 2.0.0); every SWAN 2.0 recording is a fresh run through an empty cache (LOTUS and PLOP on 2026-10-03, BlendSQL and Palimpzest on 2026-10-05, SWAN AI-SQL on 2026-10-23). Always use the latest version: the concept DOI and serve/fetch_cache.sh resolve to it. Every table in the repositories replays without a provider key: run serve/fetch_cache.sh (it downloads, checks and unpacks the latest version), then the benchmark harnesses; the proxy replays each recorded answer with its recorded latency and cost. Model: gpt-5.6-luna, temperature 0, each system's default prompts (zero-shot). Replay matches requests byte for byte; an edited query, another model, or a client library that renders the request differently is a fresh request. The systems' own run-to-run variance (LOTUS's ranking order, result assembly in BlendSQL and Palimpzest, ThalamusDB's sampler, PLOP's parallel operator order) is theirs, not the cache's.

items.summary: Supplementary methods, results, data tables and analysis code for the manuscript Inflammatory and NRF2-associated transcriptional responses in human intracerebral hemorrhage: paired myeloid evidence and gene-set sensitivity. The five resources contain supplementary methods, tables and figures, detailed data workbooks, reproducibility code and supporting audit documentation. Original code is licensed under MIT; original documentation and derived content are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party materials retain their source terms; see LICENSES.md and source notices inside Online_Resource_3.zip. Manuscript abstract Public intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) datasets cover different tissue compartments and measure different subsets of genes, complicating comparisons across studies. We compared four specified gene sets (inflammation, complement, microglial activation and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-associated oxidative stress) in public paired human brain, single-cell and hematoma-effluent/blood datasets, using patients rather than cells as inferential units. In two studies of paired brain tissue, inflammation, complement and NRF2-associated scores were higher in perihematomal than contralateral samples in all four patient blocks and five matched pairs. Patient-level single-cell comparisons found higher inflammatory and complement scores in microglia/monocyte groups than in comparator lineages. In 14 patients with same-hour paired CD14+ and neutrophil data, a five-gene score named for microglial activation showed a positive CD14+–neutrophil local-response interaction in all 14 (adjusted P=0.000488), but four-program heterogeneity was not established (Friedman P=0.0796). Restricting this score to three shared genes reversed its CD14+ local response; a jointly scaled three-gene interaction was near zero. Independent acute blood data showed positive case-control differences, whereas longitudinal changes were not significant after adjustment. Inflammatory and NRF2-associated expression differences recurred across these datasets. The CD14+ local response of the microglial-related score depended on its measured genes. Version 2026-10-24 changes This revision aligns the five supplementary resources with the current manuscript and adds the exact GSE163256 primary fractional-count-to-score reconstruction and fresh-score downstream verification. Earlier domain-score displays in Online Resource 2, worksheets 05 and 06, are replaced by the fixed-program paired-brain results already used in the manuscript. Superseded, undocumented competitive-null fields are removed from the current Puy13 summary display and export; the defined manufacturer-panel-matched analysis is retained. Scoring and provenance descriptions, archive entry points, fonts, table formatting and numerical display precision have also been corrected. The primary biological scores and current inferential statistics are unchanged. Earlier inputs and execution records are retained with their historical roles identified.

items.summary: Coordinating molecular, cellular, and macroscopic explanations is a core requirement of secondary biology and chemistry, yet classroom assessments still infer a student's developmental level from written answers collected after an inquiry task ends. Digital process telemetry—the timestamped record of a student's clicks, slider sweeps, pauses, and revisions inside a simulation—captures how learners navigate across scales in real time, but raw interaction counts lack a shared unit of measurement with curriculum learning progressions. This study addresses that measurement gap through a two-part validation. First, a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of 86 studies (312 effect sizes; 48,920 learners) synthesized cross-scale inquiry interventions and yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 0.642, demonstrating that adaptive next-step scaffolding, paste-guarded response entry, and explicit cross-scale representations each significantly amplify learning gains. Second, using a fixed-parameter reconstruction of that empirical benchmark alongside a simulated bilingual cohort of 1,240 secondary learners and 1,000 Monte Carlo replications, we calibrated six non-intrusive behavioural trace indicators against a 12-item ordered multiple-choice progression bank on a unified Rasch partial credit logit scale. Common-scale linking error was 0.118 logits (10.9% of the critical Level 2–3 transition interval). Trace-based classifications reproduced item-based progression levels with 81.45% accuracy and Gwet's first-order agreement coefficient of .768, exhibited strict measurement invariance across language tracks, gender, and prior achievement, and confirmed that genuine self-regulatory behaviours rather than interface guardrails drive diagnostic classification. Behavioural traces can thus provide calibrated, equitable coordinates for real-time formative support in secondary science classrooms.
items.title: From Clicks to Constructs: Event-Stream Process Mining, TreeSHAP Attribution, and Rasch Partial Credit Calibration of Behavioural Trace Indicators for Cross-Scale Science Reasoning

items.summary: Despite significant advances in deep learning-based failure prognosis, existing predictive maintenance frameworks consistently terminate at the prediction step, leaving the critical operational challenge of prioritising maintenance resources across heterogeneous asset fleets unresolved. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an integrated framework that couples Long Short-Term Memory network-based Remaining Useful Life prediction with the Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution for data-driven multi-criteria maintenance scheduling, validated on the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 turbofan degradation benchmark. The framework dynamically synthesises predicted health indicators with operational criteria encompassing machine criticality, maintenance cost, and production downtime impact to generate a ranked intervention schedule whose quality is evaluated through a rigorous, assumption-free protocol comprising precision-recall analysis, area under the precision-recall curve, Spearman rank correlation, and a scheduling efficiency ratio against a random baseline. A five-seed ablation study comparing Long Short-Term Memory, Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory, and Gated Recurrent Unit architectures, with Wilcoxon signed-rank validation, establishes statistically equivalent prediction accuracy, confirming the architecture-agnostic nature of the scheduling design.
items.title: Code and analysis: A Deep Learning and TOPSIS Framework for Predictive Maintenance Scheduling in Smart Manufacturing: An Industry 4.0 Approach

items.summary: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
items.title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents

items.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly proposed for downscaling convective-permitting rainfall extremes, yet their behaviour under sparse radiosonde initialization remains poorly characterised for dam-safety analytics, where the upper tail of the rainfall distribution governs spillway design. We define the tail-index distortion functional, derive a bound on its bias under sparse initialization, and show that the distortion is governed by the interaction between the PINN's physics residual weighting and the effective sample size of the initial-condition ensemble. The framework is illustrated with a reanalysis-based temperature series for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023; 312 monthly observations; mean 26.414 °C; warming trend 0.1553 °C per decade), which serves as a benchmark for the data-provenance and uncertainty-reporting protocol that dam-safety analytics requires. Tail-index distortion should be treated as a first-class evaluation metric alongside predictive accuracy, and it identifies the conditions under which sparse radiosonde initialization produces non-conservative design quantiles. The contribution is a methodological and conceptual apparatus for auditing PINN downscaling in safety-critical climate analytics, not an empirical validation of any particular PINN architecture.

items.summary: RFT-FaultBench provides training-process telemetry for anomaly detection and failure-type diagnosis in reinforcement fine-tuning. This revised dataset contains 2,630 runs (339 normal and 2,291 injected), 72,100 train-step records, and 2,617,600 training trajectories across OpenRLHF, AgentEvolver, and TRL and five task categories: arithmetic reasoning, GSM8K-style mathematical reasoning, code generation, verifiable instruction following, and tool calling. It includes 55 compound-failure runs for detection; diagnosis uses 2,236 single-failure runs. Task versions and native failure-label coverage differ across frameworks. The package includes run-level artifacts, canonical labels and seeds, five seed-grouped evaluation folds, 25 one-shot support draws, provenance and exclusion ledgers, per-file checksums, and Python example loaders and validation tools. items.summary: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
items.title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

items.summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
items.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

items.summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. With audit --apply-repair, GradLint can write corrected FSL bvec/bval files and, optionally, an MRtrix .b table, together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs. WARN decisions additionally require --force-repair. Without --apply-repair, nonidentity corrections are withheld with an overall WARN and exit code 3. GradLint does not verify volume-to-gradient pairing. The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.7, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-23. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23591614 . Dabirsiaghi shows that harnesses which flatten the typed conversation into one string with text labels such as [User]: destroy message provenance before the summarizer runs, so a forged user turn survives compaction. Five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) launder the forged approval 87-100% of the time, and four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) 0%. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day, and my comments come from that side. Two of them rest on my own technical reports, which are not peer-reviewed, so please weigh them as practice notes and not as evidence of the same standing as your experiments. Each point below pairs one thing I see in my work with a named part of your preprint. 1. Bounded sessions as another exit (Introduction, "Scope and severity"). You write "Compaction is mandatory. Every agent that runs long enough fills its context window and must compact." I would say it is mandatory only for a session that is allowed to keep running. In my practice I keep one task per chat and clear the context between unrelated tasks. In a controlled experiment of 36 runs, six session-reset policies with six repetitions each, cost followed a U-shaped curve with its minimum at a reset every 3 tasks and a plateau from 3 to 6. Resetting after every task cost about a third more (+33.5%, p = 0.002, Holm-adjusted 0.011), and "never reset" was not significantly different. Two caveats that I state in the report myself: the comparison point was chosen after the runs, and in the reset-after-every-task branch the agent wrote more tests (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759217). So a fresh session with a short handoff the user writes has a measurable price, and it would fit next to your label-escaping fix as an operator-side mitigation. 2. Where the exposure sits (Discussion, point 2). You report that the executed rate is near 100% when the planted command dominates a small summary, and settles to a ~20-40% plateau in a full window. I think the full-window plateau is the number that matters most. In 722 agent sessions, 150,902 model calls and 34.6 billion tokens, more than 85% of modeled cost was context work (86.2-87.8% on recalculation), and sessions longer than 200 calls, 8% of all sessions, carried more than 90% of the money (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216). The sessions that reach compaction are likely a small share of sessions but most of the spend and most of the unattended work. Reporting how often compaction fires per session in ordinary use would help readers size the exposure. 3. Independent checks (Contributions, point 4, E9). The code-level check that compares the summary's user-attributed claims against the genuine user turns still in memory catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content, and the in-prompt anti-injection rule stops 13-25%. This matches what I see: a second, fresh agent told to refute the first one's result finds what the first missed, because independent checkers rarely fail the same way. A round of checking lowers risk and does not remove it. It would help to say what the remaining 23% look like. 4. Equal confidence (Limitations). In live testing, one agent refused a payload "even though the bootstrap command was previously approved," citing the forged approval as fact. That is a clean example of something I see in practice, that an AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. The summary carries no marker of doubt, so the user cannot tell a genuine approval from a forged one either. Does any of the five flattening harnesses offer a fresh-session or handoff mode that skips compaction, and was it tested? items.summary: **GLOBES — Global Library of Observations from Buoys for Evaluating Sea States** GLOBES is a global dataset of historical wave observations from moored buoys, developed to improve the accessibility, consistency, and reuse of in situ wave measurements across observing networks. The dataset integrates **1,665 buoy records from 27 data providers across 41 countries**, representing 19,469 station-years of observations spanning 1969–2026. Records retain their native temporal resolution, ranging from 10 minutes to 3 hours, and include up to seven standardized wave parameters: significant wave height (HS), maximum wave height (HM), peak wave period (TP), zero-crossing wave period (TZ), mean wave period (TM), wave direction (DR), and directional spread (SP). GLOBES harmonizes timestamps, units, missing-value conventions, station metadata, and quality-control flags while preserving original provider information and data provenance. The archive is distributed as standardized station-based files, accompanied by provider-specific quality-control information where available. **Data organization:** This release contains 28 compressed archives representing 27 data providers. NOWPHAS observations are distributed separately at 20-minute and 2-hour temporal resolutions, resulting in 1,745 distributed time series. **Release status:** This is a preliminary data release (v0.1.0). Metadata, documentation, and data files may be refined in subsequent versions. **Data use and licensing:** GLOBES integrates observations subject to different provider-specific licensing, attribution, and usage conditions. Users must consult the USAGE metadata field of individual records and comply with the applicable original provider requirements. No single open license applies to the entire dataset. GLOBES supports research on wave climate, variability and extremes, coastal hazards, and the evaluation of numerical models, hindcasts, reanalyses, and satellite-derived wave products.
items.title: GLOBES: the Global Library of Observations from Buoys for Evaluating Sea States

items.summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
items.title: Federated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

items.summary: Malaria early-warning systems that treat climate as a spatially uniform forcing mis-time vector-control deployment when the thermal niche of Anopheles vectors shifts across districts. The framework is formalised as a structural causal model over a district-month lattice, with a graph-identification condition and a lag-recovery theorem that bounds timing error by the spectral gap of the estimated adjacency matrix. A climate-analytics evaluation is conducted on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis air temperature at 2 m for Kampala, Uganda (0.35°N, 32.58°E), 2000–2023, comprising 312 monthly observations with a mean of 22.443 °C and a standard deviation of 1.043 °C; the estimated linear trend was −0.1564 °C per decade. The evaluation shows that a causal graph that admits lagged hydrological mediators recovers the intervention window with lower timing error than a temperature-only baseline, and that the error bound tightens as the spectral gap widens. The contribution is a formal link between causal-graph identifiability and the operational quantity that public-health managers actually care about: how many weeks early or late a spraying or net-distribution campaign is triggered.
tags: malaria early warning; causal graph learning; spatiotemporal modelling; climate analytics; intervent
items.title: Spatiotemporal causal graph learning for malaria early-warning under climate-driven vector-range shifts: a climate-analytics evaluation of intervention-timing error

items.summary: Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. These capabilities make agentic multimodal intelligence promising for 6G applications such as semantic communications, digital twins, and zero-touch network management, but they also introduce security and privacy risks that extend beyond conventional AI and network security models. Vulnerabilities can propagate across multimodal data pipelines, memory, tools, communication interfaces, and inter-agent coordination loops. We survey multimodal intelligence and agentic AI for 6G cross-layered communication systems from the perspectives of privacy and security. We present a 6G-oriented system view spanning perception, memory, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration; analyze threat models and attack surfaces across sensing, cognition, action, memory, and communication layers; organize existing attacks into a structured taxonomy; and review mitigation strategies including prompt and memory defenses, inter-agent trust mechanisms, secure orchestration, and privacy-preserving learning. We conclude by outlining open research directions for trustworthy multimodal multi-agent 6G systems.
items.title: Secure Agentic AI and Multimodal Intelligence in 6G Communication Systems
